title: Who Gets to Name Continents?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how the continents got their names, starting with the supercontinent Pangaea and its ocean Panthalassa, and Alfred Wegener's continental drift theory. They trace the breakup of Gondwana and Laurasia, then discuss Antarctica's name (John Murray, 1904), the disputed naming of America after Amerigo Vespucci (Waldseemüller's 1507 map, the Mayan-derived "Amerrique" theory), Australia's naming (Matthew Flinders vs. Seiffert/Zeiller-era 1535 map claims), and the uncertain origins of Africa, Asia and Europe. They also cover the idea that some regions don't recognize all continents. The episode closes with listener mail from a couple road tripping from Texas to Florida.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour update
segments.summary: Hosts plug tour dates in Houston and Denver, then banter about maps, Arby's, and framing maps before introducing the topic of continent names.

segments.title: Pangaea and continental drift
segments.summary: The hosts describe the supersontinent Pangaea surrounded by the ocean Panthalassa, and Alfred Wegener's 1915 continental drift theory, supported by matching coastlines, coal deposits, and fossils.

segments.title: Breakup of supercontinents and climate of Pangaea
segments.summary: Gondwana and Laurasia split apart over hundreds of millions of years, and the hosts discuss the arid interior of Pangaea and the continents still moving today.

segments.title: Continental drift mechanics and hollow Earth
segments.summary: Josh explains that tectonic plates float on magma and cause volcanoes and earthquakes, and notes that hollow Earth theories are not supported.

segments.title: What counts as a continent
segments.summary: The hosts define a true continent as a landmass surrounded by ocean, and note that Europe and Asia are not separated by water, and Russia is split across the two.

segments.title: Antarctica's name and John Murray
segments.summary: Sir John Murray, an oceanographer from the HMS Challenger expedition, named Antarctica in 1904 as the opposite of the Arctic.

segments.title: Who the Americas were named after
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Amerigo Vespucci's reputation, the 1507 Waldseemuller map that first used the name America, the Library of Congress purchase, and competing theories including a Mayan-derived word for mountains and John Cabot.

segments.title: Australia's name
segments.summary: Australia was long attributed to Matthew Flinders, who preferred it to Terra Australis. An older map by Siriaco Yakob Sumbarth from 1655 suggests the name predates him.

segments.title: Hugh Jackman and movie banter
segments.summary: Tangential conversation about Hugh Jackman playing P.T. Barnum, Gene Hackman, and John C. Reilly films.

segments.title: Origins of Africa, Asia and Europe
segments.summary: Names for Africa, Asia and Europe are undocumented; candidate origins include Berber, Latin and Greek roots, and Phoenician words for sunrise and sunset, and the Greek myth of Europa.

segments.title: Regions that do not recognize all continents
segments.summary: Some parts of the world treat the Americas as one continent and Europe and Asia as Eurasia.

segments.title: Pavement shirt and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh mentions a pavement T-shirt and a Facebook connection to Bob Nastanovich, then points listeners to the website for more geography content.

segments.title: Road tripping listener mail
segments.summary: A listener named Kim writes that she and her husband Tom, who had never listened to a podcast, got hooked on the show during a road trip from Texas to Florida.
